elements.id-string-11: It has been shown both theoretically and experimentally that most coupled oscillators undergo synchronization and phase binarization at room temperature under sub-harmonic injection locking (SHIL), irrespective of the exact physics of their auto-oscillation or coupling.
elements.id-string-12: These phase-binarized oscillators (PBOs) can be used for Ising computing, which is about heuristically solving NP-Hard combinatorial optimization problems very fast.
elements.id-string-13: The quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) has emerged as an alternative noisy intermediate scale quantum (NISQ) era algorithm for Ising computing and is very popular currently since it is gate based and needs low circuit depth for implementation.
elements.id-string-14: In this paper, we compare the performance of PBOs with that of QAOA over a wide range of graph instances of different levels of difficulty, while restricting ourselves to the NP-Hard Max-Cut problem.
elements.id-string-15: We show that for the difficult graph instances (unweighted random cubic, unweighted Erd{\"o}s R{\'e}nyi, and weighted complete graphs with relatively high number of nodes: 18-20), the success probability (probability to find the correct Max-Cut solution) of PBOs is 4-5 orders of magnitude higher than that of QAOA.
elements.id-string-16: In fact, for Erd{\"o}s R{\'e}nyi and complete graphs, success probability of QAOA drops exponentially with increase in the number of nodes of the graph (graph size), while success probability of PBO only drops linearly with the number of nodes.
elements.id-string-17: Since PBOs operate at room temperature while the quantum circuit in QAOA doesn't (it operates in milli Kelvins), our finding here on their success probability numbers makes PBOs a more attractive hardware platform for Ising computing compared to quantum approaches like QAOA.
elements.id-string-18: Since we use the very general and physics-agnostic Kuramoto model to simulate PBOs here, our result is applicable to a wide range of oscillators both based on conventional transistors and emerging nanoscale devices.
elements.id-string-19: Hence, we also compare the time to solution for PBOs based on these different device technologies in this paper.
elements.id-string-21: Coupled oscillators are known to show very interesting phase dynamics, the nature of which is often independent of the microscopic physics of the auto-oscillation or the coupling.
elements.id-string-22: As a result, generalized mathematical models like the Kuramoto model \citep{Kuramoto} and its variations (Kuramoto-Sakaguchi model \citep{Circuit5,Circuit6}, generalized Adler's equation, etc.
elements.id-string-23: \citep{Jaijeet1,Jaijeet2}) have been used to describe the dynamics.
elements.id-string-24: It has been shown analytically, as well as through numeric simulations and experiments, that the phase dynamics of various kinds of oscillators, both based on conventional electronic circuits \citep{Circuit5,Circuit6} as well as emerging nano devices like metal-to-insulator transition devices \citep{MIT1,MIT2} and spintronic devices \citep{Spin_Liu,Spin_DB1,Spin_DB2,Spin_Ashwin,Spin_Hyunsoo,Spin_Jullie2,Spin_Finocchio1,Spin_Finocchio2}, can be captured by these models.
elements.id-string-25: Subsequently, it has also been shown that these oscillators, even at room temperature, undergo phase binarization upon sub-harmonic injection locking (SHIL) \citep{Jaijeet1,Jaijeet2,Spin_Akerman1,Spin_Akerman3}.
elements.id-string-26: These phase-binarized oscillators (PBOs) have, in turn, been shown (both through experiments and simulations) to carry out Ising computing, which is about heuristically solving NP-Hard combinatorial optimization problems much faster than conventional computers can \citep{IsingComputingReview,Jaijeet2,Circuit1,Circuit2,Circuit3,Circuit4,Spin_Finocchio2,Spin_Akerman3}.
elements.id-string-27: Solving NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems is not only of interest to the theoretical computer science community but is also useful for various practical applications: delivery scheduling, flight booking, airline crew paring, VLSI design, optimization for machine learning problems, etc \citep{TOC, CombApp1, CombApp2}.
elements.id-string-28: Noisy intermediate scale quantum (NISQ) hardware is another kind of unconventional hardware proposed for Ising computing.
elements.id-string-29: The current quantum era is deemed to be the NISQ era with all gate-based quantum hardware having 50-100 noisy qubits at the maximum \citep{NISQReview}.
elements.id-string-30: Since the originally proposed quantum algorithms like Shor's algorithm and Grover's search algorithm cannot be implemented on such a moderate number of noisy qubits (either very few noiseless qubits or millions of noisy qubits are needed for their implementation), various quantum-classical hybrid algorithms suitable for the NISQ era have evolved.
elements.id-string-31: The quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) is one such NISQ-era algorithm.
elements.id-string-32: Since the quantum circuit for QAOA has shallow depth and a classical optimization algorithm is used to optimize the quantum circuit parameters (more details on this in Section II of the paper), QAOA has been shown to be very suitable for NISQ-era quantum machines \citep{NISQReview, QAOA_Farhi,QAOA_Tutorial}.
elements.id-string-33: However, the quantum circuit involved in QAOA still needs very low temperature (in milliKelvins) for operation since quantum coherence needs to be maintained for the qubits during each forward computation step using this circuit (more details in Section II).
elements.id-string-34: Compared to that, PBOs are known to operate completely at room temperature since the governing physics of auto-oscillation and coupling do not involve quantum coherence.
elements.id-string-35: Hence, PBOs are more suitable compared to QAOA hardware for building practical machines for Ising computing (also known as Ising machines).
elements.id-string-36: Additionally, if we can show that the performance of PBOs is better than that of QAOA for different combinatorial optimization problems, then we show an added advantage of PBOs over QAOA.
elements.id-string-37: Motivated by this factor, here we have compared the performance of PBOs, simulated using Kuramoto model, with that of QAOA, simulated on the Qiskit simulator, for various instances of the popular NP-Hard combinatorial optimization problem: MaxCut (defined in Section II) \citep{IsingComputingReview,Spin_Akerman3,MIT2}.
elements.id-string-38: To cover instances of different levels of difficulty, we use four kinds of graphs: three of unweighted kinds (Mobius ladder, random cubic, Erd{\"o}s R{\'e}nyi) and one of weighted kind (complete graphs) (more details in Appendix A).
elements.id-string-39: We use graph size (number of nodes) from 4 to 20.
elements.id-string-40: We show that indeed PBOs exhibit much superior performance compared to QAOA for a wide range of graph instances.
elements.id-string-41: In fact, the success probability (probability to find the correct Max-Cut solution) of PBOs is 4-5 orders of magnitude above that of QAOA for the more difficult problem instances that we have considered here: random cubic, Erd{\"o}s R{\'e}nyi, and complete graphs with relatively high number of nodes: 18-20 (Fig. ~\ref{SuccessProb}).
elements.id-string-42: This shows that PBOs can indeed provide a more suitable platform compared to QAOA for practical Ising computing.
elements.id-string-43: Since Kuramoto model is a generalized physics-agnostic model that can describe the dynamics of a wide range of oscillators (as mentioned above), our result will be applicable to a wide range of oscillators: metal-to-insulator-transition-based \citep{MIT1,MIT2}, spintronics-based \citep{Spin_Akerman1,Spin_Liu,Spin_Finocchio1,Spin_Finocchio2}, analog-and-digital-circuits based \citep{Circuit1,Circuit2,Circuit3,Circuit4,Circuit5}, etc.
elements.id-string-44: But the time to solution for different PBO-based Ising machines will be different; it will be inversely proportional to the natural frequency of operation of the particular oscillator devices in use.
elements.id-string-45: So in this paper, we have also reported our estimated time to solution (for the different graphs we considered here) for these different oscillator technologies.

elements.id-string-53: We define the Max-Cut problem formally as follows.
elements.id-string-54: Let there be a graph $G=(V,E)$ where $V$ is the set of vertices $\{1,2,3,...N\}$ and $E$ is the set of edges.
elements.id-string-55: Each member of E can be written as $(i,j)$, where $i \in V$ and $j \in V$ and $i < j$, with the mapping function C assigning a weight to each member of E.
elements.id-string-56: For an unweighted graph, $C: E \rightarrow \{0,1\} $, while for a weighted graph, $C: E \rightarrow R^{+}$.
elements.id-string-57: The problem statement of Max-Cut is that one has to select a sub-set $S$ of V ($S \subset G$) such that the following sum is maximized: $\Sigma_{e \in \delta_G(S)} C(e) $, where $\delta_G(S)=(i,j)$ with $i \in S$ and $j \in (V-S)$, or $i \in (V-S)$ and $j \in S$.
elements.id-string-58: Intuitively, when the graph is unweighted, the graph needs to be partitioned into two parts such that the number of edges which connect a node in one partition with a node in the other partition is maximised.
elements.id-string-59: This is known as the maximum cut of the graph.
elements.id-string-60: Such partitioning has been shown for a couple of Mobius Ladder graph instances (more details on the graph in Appendix A) in Fig. ~\ref{MobiusLadder}(b), with the same graphs without partitioning shown in Fig. ~\ref{MobiusLadder}(a).
elements.id-string-61: To cover a wide spectrum of problem instances and to check the efficiency of all the Ising computing algorithms we work on here on these instances, we use four kinds of graphs in this paper including Mobius ladder, as mentioned in Section I.
elements.id-string-62: More details on these four kinds of graphs are provided in Appendix A, along with images of some graph instances we have generated for this work (Fig. ~\ref{RandomCubic}, ~\ref{ErdosRenyi}).

elements.id-string-234: Thus, in this paper, we have shown that phase binarized oscillators (PBOs) offer superior performance compared to quantum approximation optimization algorithm (QAOA) for a wide range of graph instances.
elements.id-string-235: In fact, the success probability for PBOs is several orders of magnitude higher compared to QAOA for more complex graph instances.
elements.id-string-236: With PBOs and QAOA being two popular approaches for carrying out Ising computing currently, our finding here is particularly important.
elements.id-string-237: In this paper, we have also estimated the time to solution for different oscillator technologies (electronic circuit based, metal-to-insulator transition based, spintronic) for the graph instances we have considered.
elements.id-string-238: It is to be noted that another dynamic system approach exists for Ising computing apart from PBOs, which is known as coherent Ising machine (CIM) \citep{IsingComputingReview}.
elements.id-string-239: Recently, Hamerly \textit{et al} have compared the performance of CIM with that of quantum annealers for the same optimization problem instances (QAOA is an approximate gate-based variation of quantum annealing) \citep{CoherentIMvsQA}.
elements.id-string-240: They have shown experimentally that CIM exhibits superior performance compared to the D-Wave Systems quantum annealer; compared to D-Wave, CIM reportedly has orders of magnitude lower time to solution (TTS) and orders of magnitude higher success probability for complex problem instances \citep{CoherentIMvsQA}.
elements.id-string-241: Hence, our result here (success probability of PBO orders of magnitude higher than that of QAOA) is consistent with that reported by Hamerly \textit{et al} \citep{CoherentIMvsQA}, with PBO being similar to CIM (dynamic-system-based approach for Ising computing \citep{IsingComputingReview}) and QAOA being similar to quantum annealing (quantum approach for Ising computing \citep{IsingComputingReview}).
elements.id-string-242: Additionally, CIM has major disadvantages like the use of a long fibre ring cavity and a power hungry field-programmable gate array (FPGA) to implement coupling, which is not the case with PBO \citep{MIT2}.
elements.id-string-243: Hence, our result here that PBOs, just like CIM, exhibit much higher success probability compared to quantum approaches makes PBOs very attractive for Ising computing.

elements.id-string-262: Solving computationally intensive combinatorial optimization problems efficiently through emerging hardware by converting the problem to its equivalent Ising model and obtaining its ground state is known as Ising computing.
elements.id-string-263: Phase-binarized oscillators (PBO), modeled through the Kuramoto model, have been proposed for Ising computing, and various device technologies have been used thus far to experimentally implement such PBOs.
elements.id-string-264: In this paper, we show that an array of four dipole-coupled uniform-mode spin Hall nano oscillators (SHNOs) can be used to implement such PBOs and solve the NP-Hard combinatorial problem MaxCut on 4-node complete weighted graphs.
elements.id-string-265: We model the spintronic oscillators through two techniques: an approximate model for coupled magnetization dynamics of spin oscillators, and Landau Lifshitz Gilbert Slonckzweski (LLGS) equation-based more accurate magnetization dynamics modeling of such oscillators.
elements.id-string-266: Next, we compare the performance of these room-temperature-operating spin oscillators, as well as generalized PBOs, with two other alternative methods that solve the same MaxCut problem: a classical approximation algorithm, known as Goemans-Williamson's (GW) algorithm, and a Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum (NISQ) algorithm, known as Quantum Approximation Optimization Algorithm (QAOA).
elements.id-string-267: For four types of graphs, with graph size up to twenty nodes, we show that approximation ratio (AR) and success probability (SP) obtained for generalized PBOs (Kuramoto model), as well as spin oscillators, are comparable to that for GW and much higher than that of QAOA for almost all graph instances.
elements.id-string-268: Moreover, unlike GW, the time to solution (TTS) for generalized PBOs and spin oscillators does not grow with graph size for the instances we have explored.
elements.id-string-269: This can be a major advantage for PBOs in general and spin oscillators specifically for solving these types of problems, along with the accuracy of solutions they deliver.
elements.id-string-271: Solving combinatorial optimization problems is useful for various practical applications: delivery scheduling, flight booking, airline crew paring, VLSI design, optimization for machine learning problems, drug discovery, etc \cite{CombApp1,CombApp2,RingOscApp}.
elements.id-string-272: However, because of the NP-Hard nature of most of these problems, solving them accurately on a conventional classical digital computing unit consumes exponential time or resources.
elements.id-string-273: Classical approximate algorithms like Goemans-Williamson's (GW) algorithm can be implemented on such conventional computers and can solve these problems approximately.
elements.id-string-274: But the GW algorithm, when used for the Max-Cut problem (a popular NP-Hard combinatorial optimization problem that we explore here), can only offer an approximation ratio (AR) guarantee  $\approx$ 0.878 or higher \cite{GW1}.
elements.id-string-275: Also, time complexity, or time to solution (TTS), for the GW algorithm has been found to still grow polynomially with graph size (though not exponentially) \cite{GWvsSAvsCIM}.
elements.id-string-276: Various emerging computing schemes have been proposed and experimentally demonstrated recently, targeted to solve these problems more efficiently.
elements.id-string-277: Among them,  computing schemes that convert the problem to its corresponding Ising Hamiltonian \cite{NPCompleteIsingFormulation} and then find the ground state of the Hamiltonian are known as Ising computing schemes \cite{IsingComputingReview}.
elements.id-string-278: Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) is also often used for the same purpose, and it has been shown that QUBO and the Ising model are equivalent via a linear transformation of variables \cite{Spin_Akerman1}.
elements.id-string-279: Ising computing has been implemented through various emerging technologies \cite{IsingComputingReview,GWvsSAvsCIM,CoherentIMvsQA}.
elements.id-string-280: Out of them, two popular classes of technologies are:
elements.id-string-282: quantum annealing and its gate-based counterpart, meant for Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum (NISQ) computing: Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) \cite{NISQReview,QAOA_Farhi}phase-binarized oscillator (PBO) systems \cite{OscillatorIMReview}, also known as Oscillatory Neural Networks (ONN) \cite{SKONN_NCE}
elements.id-string-283: A generalized mathematical model for PBOs, known as Kuramoto model \cite{Kuramoto}, has been used to propose  Ising computing under sub-harmonic injection locking (SHIL) in reports by Wang \textit{et al} \cite{Jaijeet1,Jaijeet2}.
elements.id-string-284: Since the Kuramoto model is highly device-physics-agnostic and has been shown to describe the phase dynamics of various kinds of oscillator devices, experimental demonstrations of PBO-based Ising computing have been reported using a wide range of device technologies: electronic inductor-capacitor (LC) oscillator \cite{Jaijeet3}, electronic ring oscillator \cite{RingOscApp,ChrisKim1,ChrisKim2}, electronic Schmitt Trigger circuit \cite{NikhilShukla1,SKONN_NCE}, metal-insulator-transition device \cite{MIT1,MIT2}, etc..
elements.id-string-285: Spintronic oscillators have also been proposed recently for Ising computing \cite{Spin_Akerman1,Spin_Akerman2,Spin_Finocchio1,Spin_Finocchio2} since they offer various advantages in this regard.
elements.id-string-286: They operate at room temperature unlike quantum methods mentioned above, which need milli-Kelvins for operation \cite{NISQReview}.
elements.id-string-287: They can be coupled through various means like dipole coupling \cite{Spin_DB1,Spin_DB2,Spin_Ashwin}, spin-wave coupling \cite{Spin_Akerman1,Spin_Akerman2}, and electrical coupling \cite{Spin_Liu,Spin_Hyunsoo}.
elements.id-string-288: They operate at a very high frequency (in GHz) and consume very low energy.

elements.id-string-453: To obtain time to solution (TTS) on a given graph instance for the Kuramoto model of generalized PBOs and Slavin's model of spin oscillators, we select 10 successful trials and calculate the average time and standard deviation of that  (in nanoseconds for spin oscillators, in number of time steps for generalized PBOs) when the phases of the oscillators reach steady state (corresponding to the correct Max-Cut solution) and do not change further.
elements.id-string-454: From Fig. ~\ref{TTS1}(a), (b), we observe that TTS obtained for spin oscillators and generalized PBOs follow the same trend, i.e., while there are some peaks, TTS overall doesn't increase with graph size.
elements.id-string-455: The peaks (long TTS) correspond to oscillators going through meta-stable phases, corresponding to local minima in the energy landscape (sub-optimal partitioning of the graph essentially), and then reaching the correct solution (corresponding to global energy minimum).
elements.id-string-456: Such phase evolution for spin oscillators (obtained through solving Slavin's model) has been shown in Fig. ~\ref{TTS2} for the 10-node random cubic graph, for which a TTS peak is observed in Fig. ~\ref{TTS1}(b) for the spin oscillator case.
elements.id-string-457: The meta-stable states and sub-optimal partitionings of the graph corresponding to them are also shown in Fig. ~\ref{TTS2}.
elements.id-string-458: In contrast to that, short TTS (which is the case for most graph instances considered) corresponds to oscillators directly going to the final steady state which yields correct solution, without going through meta-stable states.
elements.id-string-459: Such phase evolution of spin oscillators has been shown for 18-node random cubic and 20-node Mobius Ladder cases in Section 6 of Supplementary Information.
elements.id-string-460: To calculate TTS for the GW algorithm, we measure the time taken for solving the SDP relaxation and one random hyperplane measurement on a conventional digital computer with the following specifications: $11^{\mathrm{th}}$ Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) $\mathrm{i}5$-$1135$ processor and $16$ $\mathrm{GB}$ memory.
elements.id-string-461: We measure 100 such times by repeating the above process for a given graph instance and report the average time (and standard deviation) in milliseconds in Fig. \ref{TTS3}(b).
elements.id-string-462: For the four kinds of graphs considered here, TTS is plotted as a function of graph size for the Kuramoto model of generalized PBOs and classical GW algorithm in Fig. ~\ref{TTS3}.
elements.id-string-463: We have not included QAOA in this comparison because the correctness of the solution for QAOA is way below satisfactory when compared to the other methods, as discussed above.
elements.id-string-464: Fig. ~\ref{TTS3}(b) shows that TTS for GW grows polynomially with graph size for all kinds of graphs, which agrees with the report by Haribara \textit{et al} \cite{GWvsSAvsCIM}.
elements.id-string-465: But the TTS of PBOs doesn't grow overall with graph size (Fig. ~\ref{TTS3}(a)), despite a few peaks that have been explained earlier.
elements.id-string-466: This trend in TTS can be a major advantage of TTS compared to GW.
elements.id-string-467: That TTS doesn't grow with graph size has been observed for optical coherent Ising machines (CIMs) as well in the report by Haribara \textit{et al} \cite{GWvsSAvsCIM}.
elements.id-string-468: But CIMs have major disadvantages like the use of a long fibre ring cavity and a power-hungry field-programmable gate array (FPGA) to implement coupling, which is not the case with spintronic oscillators \cite{MIT2}.
elements.id-string-469: Thus, our results in the paper show that spintronic oscillators are much superior to gate-based NISQ-era quantum hardware (which implements QAOA) \cite{NISQReview} for solving combinatorial optimization problems like Max-Cut.
elements.id-string-470: Not only it's true that spin oscillators work at room temperature while quantum computers need milli-Kelvins to operate \cite{NISQReview}  but also spin oscillators offer much higher solution accuracy (AR and SP) than QAOA.
elements.id-string-471: The QAOA results here, against which we have compared oscillator results, are obtained from quantum circuit simulations, without incorporating any kind of quantum decoherence/ noise.
elements.id-string-472: It has been shown that QAOA performance goes down drastically when QAOA is implemented experimentally, or experimentally bench-marked noise is incorporated in QAOA simulations \cite{QAOA_Noise,QAOA_ICQCE1,QAOA_ICQCE2}.
elements.id-string-473: In comparison to that, oscillator-based computing has been found to be much more immune to noise.
elements.id-string-474: In fact, it has been shown that noise can actually improve AR and SP for PBOs because noise helps the system get out of local minima and reach the global minimum \cite{Jaijeet1,Jaijeet2,Csaba_Noise}.
elements.id-string-475: Noise immunity is, hence, an added advantage of oscillators over QAOA.
elements.id-string-476: Our results further show that PBOs (including spin oscillators) may offer better TTS compared to classical GW algorithm, run on conventional computers and routinely used for solving combinatorial optimization problems currently.
elements.id-string-477: TTS for GW grows polynomially with graph size, while TTS for spin oscillators, and PBOs in general (modeled through the Kuramoto model), doesn't for the graph instances we have explored in this work.
